subQuestions.questionText:
Select the term in Column B that best matches the description in Column A. Each letter may be used only once.

COLUMN A:
(a) The hormone that is secreted by the corpus luteum to maintain pregnancy.
(b) The process of fusion between a sperm cell and an ovum.
(c) The cell formed from a fertilised ovum/egg cell.
(d) The shedding of the endometrium.
(e) The structure formed from a follicle in an ovary after it has released an ovum into the oviduct.
(f) A hormone that triggers ovulation.
(g) A hormone that stimulates follicle development in the ovary.
(h) The early developmental stage of an animal during pregnancy.
(i) The time period where sexual maturity is established in humans.
(j) The release of an ovum into the oviduct.

COLUMN B:
A Menstruation  B Ovulation  C Graafian follicle  D LH  E FSH  F Corpus luteum  G Puberty  H Progesterone  I Zygote  J Fertilisation  K Embryo
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) H — progesterone
(b) J — fertilisation
(c) I — zygote
(d) A — menstruation
(e) F — corpus luteum
(f) D — LH
(g) E — FSH
(h) K — embryo
(i) G — puberty
(j) B — ovulation
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1 shows the male reproductive system with numbered parts (1–10). Which numbered part in Figure 1 contains the seminiferous tubules?
A 6
B 7
C 8
D 9
(Refer to Figure 1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: B — part 7 (the testis contains the seminiferous tubules, where sperm are produced).

subQuestions.questionText:
Which numbered part(s) secrete(s) substances to make up the liquid part of semen (excluding sperm cells)?
A 7 only
B 9 only
C 9 and 10
D 7, 9 and 10
(Refer to Figure 1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: C — parts 9 and 10 (the seminal vesicle and the prostate gland secrete the fluid of semen).

subQuestions.questionText:
Which option correctly identifies the number and name of the part in Figure 1 that is cut in the procedure called a circumcision?
A 1 — Sperm duct
B 1 — Foreskin
C 5 — Sperm duct
D 5 — Foreskin
(Refer to Figure 1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: D — part 5, the foreskin (the fold of skin over the glans that is removed in circumcision).

subQuestions.questionText:
A hormone secreted by the testes in males has a negative feedback effect on the secretion of FSH in males. What will be the most likely effect of increased secretion of this hormone on a male's reproductive system?
A Decreased spermatogenesis
B Increased spermatogenesis
C Decreased secretion of testosterone
D Increased production of nutrients for sperm cells
subQuestions.memoText: A — decreased spermatogenesis: the hormone (inhibin/testosterone) inhibits FSH by negative feedback, and less FSH means less stimulation of sperm production.

options.D: Increased production of nutrients for sperm cells

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 2 is an electron micrograph of a seminiferous tubule. The actual width of the tubule between X and Y is 190 µm. What is its magnification? Choose the range that provides the answer.
A 342–395 ×
B 190–200 ×
C 2,53–2,92 ×
D 0,34–0,39 ×
(Refer to Figure 2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: A — 342–395 ×. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size; the measured image width (≈65–75 mm) ÷ 190 µm gives a value in the 342–395 × range.

subQuestions.questionText:
Select the most appropriate term from the list — Gene flow, Homologous structures, Biogeography, Gradualism, Punctuated equilibrium, Founder effect, Outbreeding, Modification by descent — that matches each example. A term may only be used once.
(a) The webbed feet of a frog and the webbed feet of a duck.
(b) A German Shepherd dog that is crossbred with a Golden Retriever dog.
(c) 90% of beetles in a population have the gene for black colouring and 10% for brown; over time the species changes and later brown beetles make up 70% of the population.
(d) Several species of a marine snail of the genus Littorina develop in a short time period after an extinction event.
(e) The prevalence of Huntington's disease in the South African Afrikaner population, who descended from a small group of Dutch colonists in the 1600s.
(f) A bird carrying pollen from a flower of a plant species across a river to another population of the same species over 100 km away.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Homologous structures
(b) Outbreeding
(c) Modification by descent
(d) Punctuated equilibrium
(e) Founder effect
(f) Gene flow
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Study Figure 3 (the female reproductive system).
(a) On Figure 3, draw in and label the endometrium.
(b) Table 1 lists contraceptive methods (Diaphragm, Intra-uterine device (IUD), Contraceptive Pill), each with a symbol. Draw each symbol on Figure 3 to show the correct placement of the contraceptive or where it acts / functions.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Endometrium drawn in the correct position (lining the uterus) and labelled (1).
(b) (3 marks): diaphragm symbol placed covering the cervix; IUD symbol placed inside the uterus; contraceptive pill symbol placed on an ovary (or acting on the cervix).

subQuestions.questionText: A tubal ligation ('tying the tubes') is a surgical procedure to prevent pregnancy in females. Explain why this procedure is a more reliable method of contraception than the contraceptive pill.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2, each developed (4 marks): tubal ligation is permanent / once-off (the tubes are cut and tied), giving continuous contraception, whereas the pill must be taken daily to be effective; tubal ligation removes the chance of human error (forgetting or missing a dose); it is a mechanical barrier not affected by hormonal changes or by other medicines, unlike the hormone-based pill; it physically prevents the sperm reaching the ovum, so fertilisation cannot occur; its effectiveness is higher (>99%).

subQuestions.questionText: A 23-year-old woman would like to have a tubal ligation. Explain ONE reason why it is unethical for a doctor to perform a tubal ligation on the woman as a means of contraception.
subQuestions.memoText: One reason explained (2 marks): she is still young and may not fully grasp the long-term consequences; the procedure is permanent and not easily reversed, and other non-permanent options exist; she may change her mind and want children later and could regret it; the doctor has a duty to avoid causing irreversible harm.

subQuestions.questionText: Erwin Chargaff analysed the base composition of DNA from several species (Table 2). For human DNA, base A = 31%, T = 31,5%, G = 19,1%, C = 18,4%; for wheat A = 26,8%, T = 27,2%, G = 22,8%, C = 23,2%; for rat A = 28,7%, T = 24,3%, G = 25,5%, C = 25,6%. Give the name of the nitrogenous base that is represented by A.
subQuestions.memoText: Adenine.

subQuestions.questionText: State ONE similarity in the composition of the complementary nitrogenous bases in all the species shown in Table 2.
subQuestions.memoText: In every species the percentage of A is approximately equal to the percentage of T, and the percentage of G is approximately equal to the percentage of C (a roughly 1:1 ratio).

subQuestions.questionText: What evidence in the data in Table 2 indicates that the DNA molecule is made up of two strands of nucleotides?
subQuestions.memoText: The equal percentages of A and T, and of G and C, show that the bases pair up (A with T, G with C), which requires two complementary strands.

subQuestions.questionText: If Chargaff had analysed RNA, state TWO differences in the data he would have observed in Table 2.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): there would be no (0%) thymine; uracil would be present instead; the base percentages would not be complementary / not in a 1:1 ratio (RNA is single-stranded); there would be far fewer bases overall (RNA is shorter than DNA).

subQuestions.questionText:
From the list of contributions to genetics — A Constructed a model to accurately describe DNA structure; B Experimented on pea plants to formulate the laws of inheritance; C Made images of DNA using X-ray crystallography — write the LETTER of the correct contribution for each scientist:
Gregor Mendel
Rosalind Franklin
James Watson
subQuestions.memoText:
Gregor Mendel — B
Rosalind Franklin — C
James Watson — A
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Study the evolutionary tree (species A–M over the last 10 million years, with species M and H shown reaching the present day). For each statement, decide whether it is A — supported, B — contradicted, or C — neither supported nor contradicted by the evolutionary tree:
1.6.1 Species D and species F became extinct more than 5 million years ago.
1.6.2 Species J and species K are more closely related than species L and species M.
1.6.3 Species K and species L share the same most recent common ancestor.
1.6.4 Convergent evolution is evident between species M and species H.
1.6.5 Climate change is the cause of divergence between species K and species L.
1.6.6 Species M and species H are still alive today and are descendants of species A.
(Refer to the evolutionary tree in the question paper.)

The table shows fossilised skulls of two extinct hominid genera — hominid A (dated 3–4 mya) and hominid B (dated 0–0,5 mya) — in underneath and side views, with the brow ridge, mandible, cranium, palate, teeth, forehead and face labelled. Label the foramen magnum on the skull of hominid A.
(Refer to the skull images in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Foramen magnum labelled — the large opening in the base of the skull (positioned towards the rear in hominid A) (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Describe the position of the foramen magnum in hominid B compared to hominid A.
(b) How does the position of the foramen magnum indicate that hominid B habitually walked upright on two legs?
(Refer to the skull images in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (1): in hominid B the foramen magnum is more centrally positioned / further forward, beneath the skull, than in hominid A.
(b) Any 2 (2 marks): this positions the skull directly above (balanced on top of) the vertebral column; it places the head's centre of gravity above the legs; this improves balance for standing and walking on two legs.

subQuestions.questionText:
(a) Provide the term that describes 'habitually walking upright on two legs'.
(b) Describe and explain TWO advantages that walking upright afforded to hominids.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Bipedalism (1).
(b) First 2 described + explained (4 marks): it freed the hands from locomotion so they could carry tools, weapons, food or offspring and perform tasks such as hunting, crafting and food preparation; it is more energy-efficient over long distances and exposes less body surface to the sun, helping hominids survive in open grassland; it let hominids stand taller and see over long grass to spot predators and food.

subQuestions.questionText:
Write in the genus name of the hominid to which each skull belongs:
Skull A
Skull B
(Refer to the skull images in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Skull A — Australopithecus (1).
Skull B — Homo (1).

subQuestions.questionText:
Construct a table of THREE differences, other than foramen magnum position, between the skulls of hominid A and hominid B. Use the labelled features to guide you. No table heading is required.
(Refer to the skull images in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks (4): row/column headings + first 3 comparative differences. Examples:
Feature | Skull A | Skull B
Brow ridge | pronounced | reduced / receded
Forehead | low / sloping | high / more vertical
Cranium | smaller | larger
Face | angled / sloping | flat / vertical
Mandible | larger / robust | smaller / more refined
Teeth | larger | smaller
Palate | U-shaped / rectangular | V-shaped / rounded

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 4 shows the brain volume of various extinct hominid species (numbered 1 to 4) against time (mya). Using Figure 4, skulls A and B, and your own knowledge, select the most appropriate brain in Figure 4 that best matches each skull. Write only the number.
Skull A
Skull B
(Refer to Figure 4 and the skull images in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Skull A — 2.
Skull B — 4.
(1 mark each; based on their ages and brain sizes)

subQuestions.questionText:
The recent South African hominid discovery Homo naledi had a brain volume of between 460 and 510 cm³ and is dated to about 300 000 years ago. Homo naledi is not drawn on Figure 4. Draw an X on Figure 4 to indicate where the brain of Homo naledi would be correctly placed.
(Refer to Figure 4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: X placed at approximately 0,3 mya on the time axis and at about 460–510 cm³ on the brain-volume axis (roughly halfway between 0 and 0,5 mya, and between 0 and 500 cm³) (2 marks).

subQuestions.questionText:
The earliest evidence of campfires is associated with the hominid to which brain number 3 in Figure 4 belongs; its fossils have been found in Africa and Asia.
(a) State TWO advantages that a campfire would provide for a hominid.
(b) Provide the scientific name of the hominid to which brain number 3 belongs.
(c) This hominid was responsible for the dispersion of modern humans across the world. Name and describe the two hypotheses for human population migration into Europe.
(d) Mitochondrial DNA is used as a line of evidence to explain human population movement. Explain why mtDNA is useful as a line of evidence.
(Refer to Figure 4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Any 2 (2 marks): protection from predators; warmth at night / in cold conditions; light at night; the ability to cook food; more time to socialise and develop language; help with tool-making.
(b) Homo erectus (1).
(c) (4 marks): Multi-regional hypothesis — modern humans evolved simultaneously and independently in different regions (e.g. in Europe) from earlier Homo erectus populations that had already left Africa. Out of Africa hypothesis — modern humans evolved in Africa and then migrated out, replacing the earlier hominid populations in Europe and Asia.
(d) (2 marks — 1 fact explained or any 2): mtDNA is inherited only from the mother, so maternal lineages can be traced; it mutates at a fairly constant rate, so comparing mtDNA sequences between populations shows when and where populations diverged and migrated; it does not undergo crossing over / recombination, making lineages easier to track; it degrades slowly.

subQuestions.questionText: Blombos Cave is an archaeological site on the Western Cape coast, occupied during the Middle Stone Age (100 000–70 000 years ago), where some of the earliest evidence of modern human behaviour was found (engraved ochre from 75 000 years ago, the oldest known drawing from 73 000 years ago, and perforated shell beads). It is on a cliff 34,5 m above sea level in a private reserve not open to the public, and excavation is still ongoing. Give ONE reason why caves are often suitable locations for archaeologists to study aspects of human evolution.
subQuestions.memoText: Any one: early humans lived in, sheltered in and stored items in caves (protection from predators, warmth); caves offer a stable environment with less weathering, erosion and scavenging, so material is better preserved; organic materials (bones, tools, artefacts) are more likely to survive there; caves also trap animal and plant remains that reveal the diet and environment of early humans.

subQuestions.questionText: The text states that the site is still being explored and may take another decade to study fully. Suggest THREE reasons why it will take so long to study the Blombos Cave and its archaeological evidence.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (1 mark each): it is on a private reserve, so permissions are needed; it is on a cliff, so access and moving equipment and finds is difficult and hazardous; parts of the cave fill with sand and are hard to reach, so excavation must be slow and careful; fragile evidence must be removed and handled carefully to avoid damage; the different layers must be excavated and separated carefully; finds must be studied and verified by experts; storage and preservation of finds must be arranged; teams work collaboratively; dating methods take time; heritage-site ethics may require further permissions.

subQuestions.questionText: The Blombos Cave is not open to the public. Why is this scientifically important?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2, or 1 well explained (2 marks): restricting access preserves the integrity of the site while researchers are still carefully excavating the layers; public presence would slow the work, increase erosion, and risk vandalism, theft or damage to artefacts; the cave may still hold rare or novel finds that must be protected.

subQuestions.questionText: Ochre and bead artefacts were found in Blombos Cave. Propose a reason why the use of ochre and beads could be seen as an advantage in the cultural evolution of early humans.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: they helped early humans communicate ideas and stories, strengthen social bonds and express identity or status (symbolism), which increased co-operation and survival.

subQuestions.questionText: The Bonsmara cattle breed was developed in South Africa (1937–1963) by Professor Jan Bonsma by crossbreeding local Afrikaner cattle with European Hereford and Shorthorn breeds, to combine heat tolerance, tick resistance and high meat production. What is meant by the term artificial selection?
subQuestions.memoText: 2 marks: the process by which humans deliberately breed organisms that have desirable / selected traits (choosing which individuals reproduce).

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO appropriate ethical guidelines for performing crossbreeding experiments such as those done by Professor Jan Bonsma.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): the animals must be treated humanely, with adequate food, water, shelter and veterinary care; the breeding process must avoid unnecessary suffering, distress or harm; the standards of animal-welfare organisations must be met; crossbreeding should improve traits without producing harmful genetic defects; excessive inbreeding must be monitored and prevented; the long-term impact on biodiversity and ecosystems must be considered before releasing a new breed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Suggest why the following traits from the cattle breeds used to create the Bonsmara were selected by Jan Bonsma:
(a) Heat tolerance
(b) High muscle mass
(c) Tick resistance
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (1): heat-tolerant cattle experience less heat stress, so they grow and reproduce better and can survive South Africa's hot climate.
(b) (1): higher muscle mass means a higher meat yield, which is more cost-efficient and gives the farmer greater income.
(c) (1): tick resistance reduces disease and the need for medication (fewer infestations), so fewer animals die from tick-borne diseases.

subQuestions.questionText: State FOUR reasons why the Bonsmara breed are regarded as an example of hybrid vigour.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (1 mark each): it was developed by crossbreeding several different cattle breeds; it has increased heterozygosity; it is genetically hardier with fewer genetic disorders and less susceptibility to disease; it combines the strengths of all its parent breeds; it grows faster and has higher feed efficiency than the parent breeds; it develops more muscle mass; it has higher fertility and easier calving, making herds more productive; it withstands harsh climates (heat tolerance, tick resistance).

subQuestions.questionText: During artificial selection and breeding experiments there is a risk of inbreeding. Explain why inbreeding can limit the potential for evolution in a species.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): inbreeding decreases genetic variation and increases homozygosity (individuals become genetically similar); useful, advantageous alleles may be lost; harmful recessive alleles are expressed at a higher frequency, causing genetic disorders, reduced fertility and weaker offspring; with less variation there is less for natural selection to act on, so the population is less able to adapt to environmental change.

subQuestions.questionText: Livestock are often treated with hormones to enhance growth, reproduction and milk production; in dairy cattle, recombinant bovine somatotropin (rBST), a growth hormone, is used to boost milk production. List TWO features of a hormone.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): it is a chemical substance / chemical messenger; it is produced by an endocrine gland; it is transported in the blood; it acts on specific target organs / cells; it brings about a specific response / regulates a body function; it is effective in small amounts.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 6 represents the manufacture of rBST using Escherichia coli in recombinant DNA technology (steps 1–6: the somatotropin gene is removed from a cow cell, the E. coli plasmid is cut, the gene is inserted, and the transgenic bacterium is grown in fermentation tanks and the rBST purified).
(a) Why is the E. coli bacterium at step 4 considered transgenic?
(b) Describe fully what occurs during the numbered steps to produce the transgenic E. coli bacterium.
(c) Suggest why consumers might object to drinking milk or eating meat from cows that have been treated with rBST.
(Refer to Figure 6 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (2): it contains DNA / a gene / genetic material from another species (the cow somatotropin gene).
(b) (5 marks — steps 1–4 + 1 other): step 1 — the somatotropin gene is cut out of a cow cell using a restriction enzyme (endonuclease); step 2 — the plasmid is removed from the E. coli and cut open with the same restriction enzyme; step 3 — the somatotropin gene is inserted into the plasmid and sealed in place using DNA ligase (forming a recombinant plasmid); step 4 — the recombinant plasmid is taken up by the E. coli bacterium; the transgenic bacterium then multiplies in a fermentation tank, producing rBST that is extracted and purified.
(c) Any 2 (2 marks): potential health risks / concerns for consumers; possible allergic reactions; negative health effects in the cows (e.g. increased mastitis); an objection to artificial hormones being used in farming; concern that consuming it could affect their own hormone function.

subQuestions.questionText: Bovine somatotropin is a protein hormone. Figure 7 shows a section of the mRNA sequence used to synthesise it, beginning C G A | G U A | U C C | G A U (codon 1 = CGA). Name the stage of protein synthesis that forms mRNA.
subQuestions.memoText: Transcription.

subQuestions.questionText:
Complete the table to show the DNA sequence and the tRNA anticodon for codon 1 (mRNA CGA) of the sequence in Figure 7.
DNA sequence:
tRNA anticodon:
subQuestions.memoText:
DNA sequence (template): GCT (1).
tRNA anticodon: GCU (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the consequence of a mutation that deletes the base A from mRNA codon 1.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): deleting a base causes a frameshift mutation — every codon from that point is read in a new frame; different amino acids are then placed in the chain; the polypeptide sequence is changed and the protein's function is altered or lost.

subQuestions.questionText: More mRNA molecules are synthesised in cells than tRNA molecules. Suggest a reason for this.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 fact about mRNA + 1 about tRNA (2 marks): each mRNA is gene-specific and is needed to make only one type of protein, and it is short-lived (it breaks down soon after translation); tRNA plays a general role of ferrying amino acids to the ribosome (not gene-specific) and can be re-used many times / is long-lived.

subQuestions.questionText: Ribosomes are organelles involved in protein synthesis. Describe the events of protein synthesis that occur in the ribosomes.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): the ribosome is the site where amino acids are assembled into a protein; the mRNA attaches to the ribosome and tRNAs bind to it; the ribosome reads the mRNA codons and places the amino acids in the correct order; it catalyses the formation of peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids.

subQuestions.questionText:
Column 1 gives the location of endocrine glands — A In the pancreas; B In the neck; C A gland below the hypothalamus in the brain; D On top of the kidneys. Column 2 gives hormone functions — 1 Control metabolism; 2 Promotes bonding between mother and child; 3 Decreases blood glucose levels; 4 Converts glycogen into glucose; 5 Stimulates growth of bones and muscles; 6 Increases the rate of breathing. Select the appropriate LETTER from Column 1 and matching NUMBER from Column 2 for each hormone (each letter and number used only once):
Oxytocin
Adrenalin
Glucagon
subQuestions.memoText:
Oxytocin — C, 2
Adrenalin — D, 6
Glucagon — A, 4
(1 mark per correct letter and per correct number)

subQuestions.questionText: Two Grade 12 learners drew diagrams to show crossing over during meiosis (key: paternal chromosome shaded grey, maternal chromosome white). Learner A drew a homologous pair as one all-grey chromosome and one all-white chromosome (identical chromatids within each) before crossing over; Learner B drew each chromosome with one grey and one white chromatid before crossing over. Describe what is meant by crossing over.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): the exchange of genes / segments of DNA between homologous chromosomes (between a maternal and a paternal chromatid, at the chiasmata); it takes place during meiosis and increases genetic variation.

subQuestions.questionText: Name the phase when crossing over takes place in meiosis.
subQuestions.memoText: Prophase I (prophase of meiosis I / the first / reduction division).

subQuestions.questionText: Evaluate which learner, A or B, represented the process at the start of crossing over correctly. Explain your reasoning fully by referring to the diagrams of both Learner A and Learner B.
subQuestions.memoText: Learner A is correct (compulsory) + any 4 (5 marks): Learner A drew a proper homologous pair — one entirely paternal (grey) chromosome and one entirely maternal (white) chromosome; each chromosome starts with two identical (same-colour) chromatids before crossing over; the exchange of genes then occurs between the paternal and maternal chromosomes. Learner B is incorrect: each of Learner B's chromosomes has one grey and one white chromatid, showing non-identical chromatids and variation before crossing over has even taken place; although crossing over does exchange segments between paternal and maternal chromatids, the starting chromosomes as drawn are wrong. (At least 2 facts must refer to each learner's diagram.)

subQuestions.questionText: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is a severe genetic condition caused by abnormal meiosis producing a sex cell with two copies of chromosome 18; most affected pregnancies do not survive to term and few children survive past the first year. A study linked its incidence to maternal age: 25–29 years, 0,4 per 1 000 pregnancies; 30–34 and 35–39 years, both 1,8; 40–44 years, 5,4; 45–49 years, 37; no data for 50 years and older. Identify the organ where a sex cell is produced when meiosis takes place in females.
subQuestions.memoText: The ovary.

subQuestions.questionText: Plot a suitable graph of the results from the study on the incidence of trisomy 18 pregnancies (maternal age group vs incidence rate per 1 000 pregnancies: 25–29 → 0,4; 30–34 → 1,8; 35–39 → 1,8; 40–44 → 5,4; 45–49 → 37).
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (8): title including both variables e.g. "Histogram to show the incidence rate of trisomy 18 in different maternal age groups" (1); x-axis labelled "Maternal age group (years)" (1); y-axis labelled "Incidence rate of trisomy 18 (per 1 000 pregnancies)" (1); a histogram / bar graph with equal-width bars and no gaps (1); a suitable, even scale on the axes (1); correct plotting — bars for the 25–39 groups (2), the 40–44 bar (1) and the 45–49 bar (1). (A bar graph is acceptable.)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest a hypothesis that could explain the observed trend shown by the data.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks (variables identified + relationship stated + a suggested explanation), e.g.: "The incidence rate of trisomy 18 increases as maternal age increases, because meiosis in the ovaries becomes less reliable with age (e.g. deterioration of the meiotic spindle), raising the chance of non-disjunction of chromosome 18." Accept other reasonable phrasings.

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest why there is no data for the incidence rate of trisomy 18 for women over 50 years of age.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): women over 50 have usually reached menopause / are past child-bearing age; fertility is very low and there are few or no viable eggs; so there are too few pregnancies in this age group to collect meaningful data.

subQuestions.questionText: Name another example of a trisomy disorder that you have studied.
subQuestions.memoText: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21). Accept Patau syndrome (trisomy 13), Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) or Triple X (XXX).

subQuestions.questionText:
Genetic testing for a trisomy pregnancy uses amniocentesis (Figure 8): guided by ultrasound, a syringe needle is inserted to extract fluid (labelled X) from around the foetus, and a karyotype is made from the foetal cells in the fluid. It is usually done between weeks 14 and 20; done before week 14 it carries a higher risk of complications such as miscarriage. On Figure 8, label the part of the female reproductive system that is also known as the birth canal.
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: The vagina — correctly identified on the diagram (label line touching the correct part) (2 marks).

subQuestions.questionText:
A liquid (labelled X in Figure 8) is drawn into the syringe during amniocentesis.
(a) State the name of this liquid X.
(b) Explain ONE way in which liquid X protects the foetus during pregnancy.
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Amniotic fluid (1).
(b) One fact explained (2 marks): it cushions the foetus / absorbs shock, reducing the impact of external forces; it keeps the temperature around the foetus stable (insulation); it prevents dehydration, supporting growth; it provides a sterile environment, creating a barrier against harmful microorganisms; it allows the foetus to move freely, aiding circulation and preventing deformities.

subQuestions.questionText:
Suggest why the process of amniocentesis in an early pregnancy, before week 14, may carry a high risk of miscarriage. In your answer refer to specific names and numbered parts in Figure 8.
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Must mention a correctly numbered/named part + its state before week 14 + a reason for the miscarriage risk (4 marks): before week 14 the uterus and amniotic sac are small, so it is hard to insert the needle safely without touching the foetus; the foetus is still forming its major organs, so any needle damage to the umbilical cord, amniotic sac or foetus is dangerous; the placenta is small and could be disturbed, disrupting its hormone production; the needle can irritate the uterus and cause cramping, leading to shedding of the endometrium.

subQuestions.questionText:
Structure 4 in Figure 8 contains blood vessels. Complete the table: provide a heading that identifies structure 4; name the type of blood vessels found in structure 4; and state a function of each blood vessel found in structure 4.
(Refer to Figure 8 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Heading: e.g. "Table to show the blood vessels in the umbilical cord" (1).
Artery — carries deoxygenated blood / metabolic wastes / carbon dioxide from the foetus to the placenta (1–2).
Vein — carries oxygenated blood / nutrients from the placenta to the foetus (1–2).

subQuestions.questionText:
A karyotype of a normal healthy foetus is shown.
(a) Change the karyotype to accurately represent a trisomy 18 karyotype by drawing in the extra chromosome(s).
(b) Does the karyotype indicate a male or a female foetus? Give a reason for your answer.
(Refer to the karyotype in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) (2 marks): an extra chromosome drawn only at the chromosome 18 position (making three), the same length and width as the existing chromosome 18s.
(b) (2 marks): female — there are two X chromosomes and no Y chromosome.

subQuestions.questionText: Parus major (the great tit) has a black head, white cheeks, olive upperparts and yellow underparts; the male's breast colour correlates with stronger sperm and signals his reproductive superiority. Carotenoids increase the yellow intensity of the breast but cannot be synthesised by the bird and must come from food; females select males with brighter breasts and wider ventral stripes. Explain why access to healthy food sources is important for the male Parus major birds to ensure reproductive success.
subQuestions.memoText: 3 marks (1 fact each: access to food + effect on the male + link to reproductive success): birds cannot make carotenoids and must obtain them from food; more carotenoids in the diet make the male's yellow breast brighter (and brighter colour correlates with stronger sperm); females preferentially select and mate with brighter-breasted, wider-striped males, so a well-fed male is more likely to mate and reproduce.

subQuestions.questionText:
For each row, decide which item(s) describe Parus major, using: A — only item 1; B — only item 2; C — both; D — neither.
(a) 1. Parus major is viviparous. 2. Parus major is ovoviviparous.
(b) 1. Parental care present. 2. Parental care absent.
(c) 1. Monogamous breeding pairs are common in Parus major. 2. Breeding outside of the Parus major monogamous pairs is evident.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) D — great tits are oviparous (they lay eggs), so neither item applies.
(b) A — parental care is present (both parents raise the chicks).
(c) C — both: monogamous pairs are common and extra-pair copulations also occur.
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify a reproductive strategy of Parus major described in the text and explain how this reproductive strategy can increase its reproductive success.
subQuestions.memoText: Name a strategy + one explained fact (3 marks). Examples: internal fertilisation — sperm is deposited inside the female's tract, so more sperm reaches the egg and less is lost to the environment or predators; ovipary — the egg contains yolk and albumen so the chick is well developed at hatching, and the shell protects it so more eggs hatch; parental care — parents build nests, incubate eggs and feed the chicks, improving offspring survival; courtship / display — females choose brighter, healthier males, so offspring inherit 'good genes' and stronger traits.

subQuestions.questionText: The average lifespan of Parus major is around 3 years. Mortality is around 50% within the first month and then declines at a relatively constant rate through the rest of its life. Sketch the appropriate survivorship curve for Parus major on the axes provided. Include a suitable scale and labels for the axes.
subQuestions.memoText: Marks (4): suitable scale on both axes (1); axes labelled — x-axis "(Average) lifespan (years)", y-axis "Percentage survivorship" (1); a Type II / Type III-leaning curve — a sharp drop from 100% to about 50% within the first month, then a roughly steady decline from 50% to 0% by 3 years (2).

subQuestions.questionText: Parus major in England (Population A) have evolved beaks about half a millimetre longer than those in the Netherlands (Populations B and C); over the past 26 years the English birds' beaks have lengthened by about a tenth of a millimetre, thought to be due to the widespread use of deep-access bird feeders in English gardens (Figure 10). What is the meaning of the term species?
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (3 marks): a group of organisms of common ancestry / genetic origin; that resemble one another (look similar); that are able to interbreed; to produce fertile offspring.

subQuestions.questionText:
What do the presence of the bird feeders in the area represent? Tick the correct option.
A cause of mutations
A selection pressure
A reduction in fitness
subQuestions.memoText: A selection pressure.

subQuestions.questionText: The bird feeders allow the Parus major birds access to a source of food in addition to their natural diets. By referring to Darwin's theory of natural selection, explain how the longer-beaked Parus major birds in Population A were able to evolve in 26 years.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (4 marks): there is genetic variation in beak length in the population; birds with longer beaks can reach the food in the deep feeders (an advantage, especially when natural food is scarce); these birds are more likely to survive and reproduce; the long-beak alleles are passed on to the next generation; over successive generations the proportion of longer-beaked birds in Population A increases.

subQuestions.questionText: Are humans driving the evolutionary change in Parus major? Give a reason for your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: One fact explained to support the decision (2 marks). YES: human activity (urbanisation, habitat fragmentation and the widespread use of bird feeders) has created a new selection pressure favouring longer beaks. OR NO: natural selection pressures such as predation, climate and competition still play a major role, and not all Parus major populations have access to bird feeders.

subQuestions.questionText: Biologists hypothesise that Population A of Parus major will become a separate species from Populations B and C in the future. Explain why this hypothesis is valid.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (2 marks): Population A is geographically separated from Populations B and C by the English Channel / North Sea, so there is little or no gene flow between them (they are reproductively isolated) — the conditions for allopatric speciation; Population A also faces different selection pressures, so different alleles are selected for and the populations diverge genetically over time until they can no longer interbreed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Scientists found that beak length in Parus major is polygenic, but one gene affecting beak length is under strong selection; it has two alleles, D and d, and the d allele (associated with longer beaks) is at a much higher frequency in the English population. For each statement, write the term used in the text that matches it:
(a) A contrasting version of a gene.
(b) Controlled by many genes.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Allele (1).
(b) Polygenic (1).

subQuestions.questionText: The allele 'd' for longer beak length is recessive. What is meant by the term recessive?
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: an allele that is only expressed in the phenotype when two copies are present (homozygous); its effect is masked when the dominant allele is also present.

subQuestions.questionText: Breeding experiments with the same pair of Parus major birds repeatedly produced offspring that were 50% long-beaked and 50% short-beaked. Use a Punnett diagram to show the genetic cross between this pair. Include the parental genotypes, the Punnett diagram, and the possible genotypes of the offspring. Key: short-beaked = D, long-beaked = d.
subQuestions.memoText:
Parental genotypes: Dd × dd (2).
Punnett square: gametes D, d (from Dd) and d, d (from dd) giving Dd, dd, Dd, dd (2).
Offspring genotypes: 1 Dd (short-beaked) : 1 dd (long-beaked) — a 50:50 ratio (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Sunflowers (Asteraceae) form a compound head made of ray flowers around the edge and many complete disc flowers in the centre; only the pollinated disc flowers produce seeds (Figure 12). The ray flowers are sterile and do not produce gametes. Suggest a role that ray flowers play in sexual reproduction.
subQuestions.memoText: 1 mark: they attract pollinators (their large, bright petals make the flower head conspicuous to insects).

subQuestions.questionText:
Name the male part of the flower that is labelled in Figure 12.
(Refer to Figure 12 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: The anther.

subQuestions.questionText: Construct a flow diagram to show the process of sexual reproduction from pollination until a seed is formed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Heading + correct sequence (starting with pollen landing on the stigma and ending with seed development, with at least 2 consecutive facts) + any 3 facts (5 marks):
• Pollen lands on the stigma of a disc flower and grows a pollen tube.
• The pollen tube grows down the style.
• The male gamete is released from the pollen tube into the ovule.
• The male gamete fuses with the female gamete (fertilisation) in the ovule.
• The fertilised ovule develops into a seed.
